transcript.content: Hello

Hello Brenda, it's good to see you again. Thanks for reaching out today.

How have things been going since we last connected? Is there anything specific on your mind that you'd like to talk about, or anywhere you'd like us to start today?

I’ve been… kind of stuck. Like, I keep thinking about the same few things over and over. The garage work feels heavier lately, and I’ve been avoiding calling in sick, but I’m not sure how much longer I can keep up.  

I didn’t sleep well again last night. Laid there for ages, mind racing about little stuff—like if I left the oven on, or if I said something off about the oil change yesterday. It’s not even that big a deal, but I keep replaying it like it matters.  

I don’t know if I’m just tired, or if this is worse than before. I feel like I’m running on empty, and the thought of doing anything—like laundry, or even just making a meal—feels like too much.  

I guess I’m just… not sure what to do with it.

Brenda, thank you for sharing all of that with me. I can hear how much effort it's taking just to keep things going, and I want you to know — what you're describing makes sense, and it sounds really exhausting.

A few things stand out to me in what you said. The racing thoughts at night, replaying small moments during the day, work feeling heavier, and even basic tasks like laundry or meals feeling like too much — that's a lot to carry, especially on 5-6 hours of sleep.

I also hear you questioning whether this is "just tired" or something more. The fact that you're noticing it and bringing it up here tells me something in you recognizes this might be more than ordinary fatigue.

Can I ask — when you say you're "not sure how much longer you can keep up," what does that mean for you? Are you feeling like you might need to step back from work, or is there something else underneath that?

I want to make sure I understand where you are right now, because you matter, and I don't want to gloss over anything you're trying to tell me.

I don’t know if I can keep doing this job much longer. Not because I don’t like fixing cars — I do, in theory. But every time someone questions me, or even just looks at me like they’re waiting for me to explain something, I freeze. Like my brain just shuts down.  

I’ve been calling in sick twice this week. I didn’t even mean to. I just… woke up and couldn’t move. Not physically, but like, my body was there, but I wasn’t. I lay in bed for an hour, trying to get up, but the thought of showering, getting dressed, driving — it all felt like climbing a wall.  

And I don’t want to lose my job. I need the money. But I also don’t want to keep pretending I’m okay when I’m not. I don’t even know what “okay” means anymore.  

I guess what I’m saying is… I don’t know how to fix it. Not the work stuff, not the sleep, not the thoughts. I’ve tried. I’ve sat still for five minutes. I’ve walked around the yard. I’ve even opened a mindfulness app. But it’s like my mind won’t stop. It just keeps looping.  

I don’t want to be like this. I really don’t. But I don’t know how to stop.

Brenda, I really hear you. And I want to pause on something important — you said "I don't want to be like this," like there's something you're doing wrong. But what you're describing — the freezing, the mornings where you can't get moving, the looping thoughts, the sleep — those are symptoms. They're not a character flaw, and they're not a failure of willpower. They're signals that your mind and body are overwhelmed, and they're asking for something more than willpower can give.

And I want to acknowledge something else: you *have* been trying. You sat still. You walked. You opened an app. That's not nothing — that's you reaching for tools even while running on empty. The fact that they didn't work doesn't mean you failed. It might mean the tools you need right now are different, or bigger, than what you've tried.

The freezing at work when someone questions you — that sounds really disorienting, especially in a field where you're probably already having to prove yourself. Can I ask — has something specific happened recently that started this pattern, or has it been building for a while?

And one more thing I want to check on, because I care about your safety. When you say you don't know how much longer you can keep up — are you having any thoughts about hurting yourself, or about not wanting to be here? I want to make sure I'm hearing you fully, not just the parts that feel easier to say.

I don’t want to hurt myself. I really don’t. But sometimes, when I’m lying in bed and the silence is too loud, I think about what it would be like to just… stop. Not forever, just for a little while. Like, if I could just close my eyes and not have to think about what I said, or what I forgot, or if I’ll be able to get through the day.  

It’s not a plan. It’s not something I want to do. It’s just… a thought that comes up when everything feels too heavy.  

But I do know I’m not ready to give up. I don’t want to. I just don’t know how to get through it.  

And the thing is — it’s not one thing. It’s not like someone said something mean. It’s the way I keep thinking about every little thing. Like, yesterday, I had to replace a brake line. I did it right. But after, I kept wondering if I missed a step, if I didn’t tighten it enough. I kept going back to the car in my head, checking it over and over. I didn’t even go to the shop today. I just stayed home.  

I don’t know if I can keep doing this. But I also don’t know how to stop.

Brenda, thank you for being so honest with me about those thoughts. I know that took courage. And I want you to hear this clearly — the fact that you can tell me you don't want to hurt yourself, that you know you're not ready to give up, that matters. Those thoughts about wanting to just stop and rest — they're more common than people think, especially when someone is carrying as much as you are. They're a sign of exhaustion, not of weakness.

I also want to say — you didn't go to the shop today. That's the third time this week. And I'm not saying that to make you feel guilty. I'm saying it because I think it tells us something important about where you are right now. Your body and mind are telling you they need something, and pushing harder isn't working.

The brake line thing — you did it right, and you *knew* you did it right, but your mind wouldn't let you trust it. That loop of going back and checking, replaying it — that sounds exhausting. And it sounds like it's happening with a lot of things, not just work.

I think something I want to be real with you about is this: what you're describing — the looping thoughts, the freezing, the mornings where you can't move, the sleep, the thoughts about wanting to stop — this is beyond what mindfulness apps and walks in the yard are going to solve. Not because those things are bad, but because you might need more support right now. And that's okay.

Can I ask — do you have a doctor or a therapist you could talk to? Someone who could help you figure out what's going on and what might help?

I’ve been meaning to. I really have. But every time I try to call, I just… freeze. Like, I’ll open the app, type in “mental health,” and then stop. I don’t know what to say. I don’t even know if I’m “bad enough” to need help.  

I don’t want to be a burden. I don’t want to be the one who “can’t handle it.” I’ve always been the one who fixes things. I’m the one who can fix a transmission, who can figure out why the engine won’t start. But I can’t fix this.  

And I don’t know how to explain it. I don’t even know what’s wrong. I just feel… stuck. Like I’m running in place, and no matter how hard I push, I’m not getting anywhere.  

But I don’t want to keep going like this. I don’t want to keep missing work. I don’t want to keep lying in bed and thinking about every small thing I said or didn’t say.  

I just don’t know how to start.

Brenda, I want you to hear something: you just did the hardest part. You told me what's wrong. You told me you're stuck, that you can't fix this, that you don't want to keep going like this. That's not "not bad enough." That's someone telling me she's drowning in a river and asking if there's a rope.

You don't have to know the clinical words. You don't have to have it figured out. When you call, you can literally say what you just said to me — "I've been missing work, I can't sleep, my thoughts won't stop, and I need help." That's enough. That's more than enough.

And the freeze when you try to make the call — that's the same freeze that happens at work. It's not avoidance or laziness. It's your nervous system saying "this feels too big." So let's make it smaller.

What if you didn't have to call? What if you could write an email or use an online booking form? Or even ask a roommate to sit with you while you make the call?

And one more thing — you said you can fix a transmission but you can't fix this. But you wouldn't expect a transmission to fix itself, would you? You'd use tools, get help, maybe bring in someone with a different specialty. This is the same thing. Asking for help isn't being the one who "can't handle it." It's being the one who's smart enough to use the right tool.

Would you be willing to take one small step this week — even just looking up one provider's name and number? Not calling yet. Just finding it.

I think I can do that. Just… look it up. Not call. Not even think about what I’ll say. Just find a name.  

I don’t know why that feels so hard. Like my hands won’t move. But I keep thinking about what you said — about not having to fix it all at once. That helps a little.  

I’ll do it tonight. After dinner. When the house is quiet. I’ll open my phone, type in “mental health therapist near me,” and just… look.  

I don’t know if I’ll follow through. But I’ll at least do that. Just the name. Just the number.  

And if I don’t, I’ll tell you. I won’t pretend I did. But I’ll try.

Brenda, that's enough. That's genuinely enough for right now. And the fact that you're being honest about the uncertainty — that you might not follow through, and you won't pretend — that tells me a lot about you. That's integrity. That's someone who wants to do this right, not just look like she's doing it.

One small thing that might help: when you find the name and number, write it down somewhere. On paper, not just in your phone. There's something about physically writing it that makes it a little more real, a little more yours. And then you're done. That's the whole task. No calling, no planning, no rehearsing what to say. Just the name and the number.

And if your hands won't move tonight, that's okay too. We can talk about what got in the way. No shame, no pressure. Just curiosity about what happened.

I also want to leave you with something before we wrap up. You're in a really hard place right now, and if things ever feel like they're tipping from "I want to stop for a while" to something more, I need you to have a safety net. **988** is the crisis line — you can call or text it, and you don't have to be in immediate danger to use it. You can call just because everything feels too heavy and you need someone to talk to. Okay?

You came in today and you told me the truth. All of it. The work, the sleep, the thoughts, the freezing. That's not someone who "can't handle it." That's someone handling it, one piece at a time.

Same time next week?

Okay. I’ll try to do it. Write it down. On paper.  

And I’ll remember 988. I’ll keep it in my phone. I don’t know if I’ll use it. But I’ll know it’s there.  

Same time next week. I’ll be here. If I can.  

Thank you.

You don't need to thank me, Brenda. You showed up today and told the truth when everything in you was telling you to hide it. That took more courage than you're giving yourself credit for.

Just the name. Just the number. On paper. That's all.

And I'll be here next week. No matter what. If you find the number, great. If you don't, we'll figure out what happened together. Either way, you're not doing this alone.

Take care of yourself tonight. Even if that just means eating something and going to bed. That counts too.

See you next week, Brenda.

Okay. I’ll try.  

I’ll eat something. Maybe a sandwich. And I’ll go to bed.  

I’ll remember.  

See you next week.

A sandwich counts. Sleep counts. Showing up next week counts.

You don't have to do more than that tonight.

See you next week, Brenda.

Okay.  

Thanks.
Take care, Brenda. Talk soon.
Goodnight.
Goodnight, Brenda. Rest well.
I’ll try.
